question: What primary body system does an intravenous pyelogram evaluate?
explanation: An intravenous pyelogram uses contrast media to visualize the kidneys, ureters, and bladder, which make up the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is an iodinated contrast medium administered during an IVP?

options.A: To make the urinary structures visible on X-ray imaging
options.B: To stimulate rapid glomerular filtration beyond normal rates
options.C: To permanently stain the renal parenchyma for laboratory biopsy
options.D: To completely paralyze peristalsis within the ureteral walls

explanation: Iodine blocks X-rays, making the fluid-filled urinary tract radiopaque and clearly outlineable on radiographic films. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which clinical finding is a classic indication for scheduling an intravenous pyelogram?

options.C: Acute inflammation of the gastric mucosa

explanation: Blood in the urine often prompts visualization of the renal collecting system and ureters to rule out stones, tumors, or structural bleeding sites. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: A patient presents with recurrent flank pain and a history of passing small mineral deposits. Which diagnostic imaging test is specifically tailored to trace the entire urinary drainage tree using radiopaque dye?
explanation: An IVP is uniquely designed to highlight stones and structural changes within the kidneys, ureters, and bladder via excreted contrast media. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: What pre-existing condition places a patient at the highest risk for contrast-induced nephropathy during an IVP?
explanation: Pre-existing kidney disease reduces the clearance of heavy iodinated contrast, increasing susceptibility to further renal tubular damage. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard contraindication or safety concern for an intravenous pyelogram?

options.A: Elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.B: Known severe allergy to iodinated contrast agents
options.C: Confirmed or suspected early stage pregnancy
options.D: Routine consumption of a high-fiber diet

explanation: Dietary fiber does not interfere with iodinated contrast media or radiation safety, whereas allergies, renal impairment, and pregnancy are major clinical concerns. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is bowel preparation necessary prior to an intravenous pyelogram?

options.A: To prevent gas and stool from obscuring the kidneys and ureters
options.B: To stimulate rapid excretion of the contrast medium by the liver
options.C: To lower systemic blood pressure before the intravenous access is set
options.D: To prevent the patient from experiencing nausea during dye injection

explanation: Feces and gas cast shadows on X-ray films that can easily hide small renal stones or subtle ureteral irregularities. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient scheduled for an IVP mentions a severe past allergic reaction to shellfish. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Administer an extra dose of oral laxative to speed up digestion
options.B: Proceed with the scheduled injection because shellfish allergies are unrelated
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink two liters of plain water right away
options.D: Notify the radiology department and attending physician immediately

explanation: Shellfish allergy is often associated with sensitivity to iodine contained in contrast media, requiring medical review for premedication or alternative imaging. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the purpose of the initial KUB radiograph taken at the beginning of an IVP procedure?

options.A: To check for pre-existing radiopaque stones and verify bowel preparation
options.B: To measure the exact volume of residual urine remaining in the bladder
options.C: To deliver a therapeutic dose of radiation to the renal parenchyma
options.D: To test the patency of the peripheral intravenous catheter line

explanation: The baseline KUB ensures that intestinal gas or stool is minimized and identifies any stones that would already be visible without contrast. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why are abdominal compression bands sometimes applied during the middle phase of an intravenous pyelogram?

options.A: To physically crush small kidney stones trapped inside the lower ureters
options.B: To stimulate immediate peristaltic contractions in the urinary bladder wall
options.C: To delay the drainage of contrast and enhance visualization of the renal pelvis
options.D: To prevent the patient from moving their lower extremities during exposures

explanation: Compression temporarily slows urine flow down the ureters, allowing the renal calyces and pelvis to fill and dilate for sharper images. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: What common, transient sensation do many patients report immediately after the intravenous injection of contrast dye?

options.A: Sudden numbness and tingling in both lower legs
options.B: A temporary metallic taste and feeling of warmth
options.C: Complete temporary loss of peripheral vision
options.D: Severe cramping pain in the upper right abdomen

explanation: A transient flush and metallic taste are typical, benign side effects experienced as the iodine circulates through the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for encouraging high fluid intake following the completion of an IVP?

options.A: To prevent the development of chronic urinary tract infections
options.B: To replace electrolytes lost during the mandatory bowel preparation
options.C: To expand total blood volume and prevent orthostatic hypotension
options.D: To facilitate the rapid clearance of contrast media from the kidneys

explanation: Ample fluids help dilute and flush the nephrotoxic iodinated contrast out of the renal system quickly, minimizing potential kidney stress. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the immediate priority nursing action when a patient begins displaying signs of severe anaphylaxis during contrast injection?

options.A: Ask the patient to describe their medical history
options.B: Offer the patient a glass of cold water
options.C: Document the exact time the reaction started

explanation: Stopping the influx of the offending allergen is always the first life-saving intervention before administering emergency drugs. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: Which medication is considered the primary, frontline emergency drug for treating acute laryngeal edema and severe bronchospasm caused by contrast media?
explanation: Epinephrine rapidly reverses severe allergic bronchospasm and vasoconstriction during anaphylactic shock. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: What term describes the abnormal radiographic finding of a dilated renal pelvis and calyces seen on an IVP?
explanation: Hydronephrosis refers to the swelling of the kidneys due to a backup of urine, easily visualized on IVP as enlarged, dilated collecting structures. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)

question: An IVP series reveals that one kidney fails to excrete and concentrate the contrast medium even after thirty minutes, while the contralateral side functions normally. What is the most likely clinical implication?

options.A: Unilateral renal obstruction or severe vascular compromise on the affected side
options.B: Normal physiologic variation in urinary filtration rates between genders
options.C: Inadequate bowel preparation masking the lower abdominal structures
options.D: Bilateral congenital agenesis of the lower urinary tract system

explanation: Delayed or absent excretion on one side points directly to a blocked ureter or impaired blood supply unique to that kidney. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)
